summary: Defines the protocol IRC servers use to talk to one another, which lets many servers act together as one chat network. It is an informational memo and builds on the IRC architecture document.

plainLanguage.summary: Chat servers have to chat with each other too. This is their shared language, so a message sent to one server can reach people connected to another.

questions: how do irc servers talk to each other
what does the irc server command do
how does irc flood control work
subtitle: How IRC servers link into one tree, share who and what exists, and survive splits, floods and name clashes.

tldr.problem: A single IRC server can only serve its own users. To make a worldwide chat network, many servers must connect, relay each other's messages and agree on who is online and which channels exist.
tldr.mechanism: Servers link in a tree and each keeps a global state database. They introduce themselves with PASS and SERVER, announce users with an extended NICK message, exchange channel members with NJOIN, and clean up with SQUIT when a link breaks.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. The RFC itself admits the design scales poorly because every server must know about every other server, client and channel.

today: RFC 2813 is an Informational memo from April 2000 that updates RFC 1459. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the server-side companion to RFC 2812 and RFC 2811.

sections.title: The Global Database
sections.content:
This document is for people implementing an IRC server or an IRC service. Servers provide the three basic services required for real-time conferencing in the IRC architecture (RFC 2810): a client locator (through the client protocol, RFC 2812), message relaying (through the protocol defined here) and channel hosting and management (following RFC 2811).

Although the model looks distributed, each server keeps a global state database about the whole IRC network, which is in theory identical on every server. A server is identified by a name of at most sixty three (63) characters. A user has a unique nickname of at most nine (9) characters, and servers must also know the user's host, username and home server. A service is named by a nickname and a server name and, unlike a user, can request part or all of the global state but may not join channels. A channel known to a server requires that server to track its members and modes.

Servers can be grouped under a hostmask. Servers outside the masked area see only one virtual server named by the mask.
sections.plainLanguage: Every server keeps its own copy of the big guest list for the entire network. All the copies are supposed to match.

sections.title: Server Messages
sections.content:
Server-to-server messages use the same format as the client protocol: an optional prefix, a command and at most fifteen (15) parameters, ending in CR-LF and no longer than 512 characters. Client connections are considered untrustworthy, so they face more restrictions than server connections.

The prefix tells a server the true origin of a message. If the prefix is not in the receiving server's database, the message MUST be discarded, and if it claims to come from an unknown server the link it arrived on MUST be dropped. If the prefix is known but belongs to a different link than the one the message came in on, the receiver issues a KILL when the prefix is a client seen from a server link, and a server link MUST be dropped. Dropping a link is described as a little excessive but necessary to keep the network sound.

The extended prefix with user@host MUST NOT be used between servers. Numeric replies cannot originate from a client, and such messages are silently dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message says who it really came from. If a server gets a message from a name it has never heard of, it assumes something fishy is going on and hangs up.

sections.title: Registering Servers, Users and Services
sections.content:
PASS sets the connection password and MUST be sent before SERVER. Between servers it carries a version of four digits (this protocol is version 2.10, written as 0210), a flags string with the implementation name and a | character, and options, where Z asks for link compression and P signals anti-abuse protections.

SERVER introduces a server with its name, a hop count (local peers have 0 and each passed server adds one), a token and an info string. The token is a number that is unique only for that one link and is used afterwards by NICK and SERVICE messages. If a SERVER message introduces a server that is already known, the connection it came from MUST be closed, because a duplicate route breaks the acyclic nature of the IRC tree.

A server announces a new user with an extended NICK message that combines NICK, USER and MODE and carries nickname, hop count, username, host, server token, user mode and real name. SERVICE introduces a service, with a distribution mask limiting which servers know of it. This form of NICK MUST NOT be accepted from user connections.
sections.plainLanguage: When two servers meet they show a password and an ID card, say how far away they are, and give a pocket number to use as shorthand. They also announce each new visitor in one tidy message.

sections.title: Linking, Splitting and Channel Messages
sections.content:
After a server receives a valid PASS/SERVER pair it SHOULD reply with its own, followed by all the state it knows. The required order is: all known servers, then all known clients, then all known channels. Servers go first so that server collisions appear before any nickname collisions. Because an IRC network can only be an acyclic graph, the place where a server collision occurs shows where the network needs to split. Channel topics SHOULD NOT be exchanged, since TOPIC overwrites old information.

NJOIN is used only between servers and lists the members of a channel when two servers connect, with @@ for the channel creator, @ for an operator and + for voice. JOIN is checked only by the user's local server and then broadcast to all servers, so each knows where channel members are.

When a link closes, whether through SQUIT or natural causes, the server that noticed MUST tell the rest of the network, sending one SQUIT for each server behind that link. This is the netsplit. A server whose peer dies must fill in the comment field with something appropriate. A server-server link X.
sections.plainLanguage: When two server towns connect they swap lists in a fixed order: first the towns, then the people, then the rooms. If a road breaks, the towns on each side announce who just went missing.

sections.title: Race Conditions, Nickname Delay and Flood Control
sections.content:
Servers are REQUIRED to keep a history of recent nickname changes, because commands such as KILL, MODE (for o and v) and KICK may arrive just after the target changed nick. The server checks the nickname, then its history to see who the nick now belongs to. This reduces race conditions but cannot remove them.

Servers SHOULD also remember nicknames released by a network split or a KILL, and keep them unavailable to local clients for a period. This Nickname Delay is said to have significantly reduced collisions and abuse. The duration should be uniform across a network.

For flood control the server keeps a message timer for each client. While the timer is less than ten (10) seconds ahead of the current time, the server parses messages and penalizes the client by two (2) seconds per message. In effect a client may send one message every two seconds without ill effect. Services are normally exempt.

To avoid blocking, servers should use non-blocking I/O, including for DNS and ident lookups, which the reference implementation does with its own routines. Servers must also poll each connection with PING to detect dead links.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers keep a notebook of recent name changes so they do not tell the wrong person off. They also slow down anyone who talks too fast, about one message every two seconds, so one noisy person cannot clog the network.

sections.title: Scaling Problems and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that this protocol does not scale well in a large arena. Every server must know about every server, client and channel, and update that information as soon as it changes. Labels such as nicknames and channel names can collide when users on different servers pick the same one. Most servers do few consistency checks and assume a neighbouring server is correct, so a buggy server can introduce contradictions into the network.

Servers have only two means of authenticating incoming connections, a plain text password and DNS lookups. The RFC calls these weak and widely recognized as unsafe, but says the combination has been sufficient in the past. Public networks accept users with few restrictions, and private networks often use their own mechanisms. Since PASS and OPER are sent in clear text, a stream encryption layer such as TLS (RFC 2246) could protect them.
sections.plainLanguage: The big guest list is hard to keep when the town gets huge, and the secret passwords are only a weak lock. The authors suggest putting the whole conversation in a sealed envelope.
